2026-02-23: Anthropic account bans: company reports investigation linked to three Chinese AI labs

Anthropic said it linked about 24,000 accounts it classified as fraudulent and more than 16 million exchanges with Claude to DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax. It described replacement accounts appearing after bans.

These are the company’s allegations and estimates about particular activity, not a count of bans by nationality. It did not say all 24,000 accounts had been banned or that all Chinese users had been suspended.
2025-09-04: Anthropic extends regional restrictions to some overseas companies

Anthropic said an organisation’s place of incorporation was not the only test for access to Claude. Its example included entities more than 50% owned, directly or indirectly, by companies headquartered in an unsupported region. It explicitly named China.
The rule affects some subsidiaries operating abroad. It concerns location and corporate control; the announcement is not a list of individual suspensions and gives no count by nationality.
2024-01-30: Northern Myanmar scams: ten suspects handed over to China

In an operation concerning scam networks in Kokang, Myanmar police handed ten suspects, including Bai Suocheng, to Chinese police. Their flight reached Kunming that evening. The date marks the handover, not the start of the scams.

Suspected organisers, fraud victims and people trafficked into forced scamming are distinct groups. The UN human rights office documented forced criminality in Southeast Asian scam compounds. This handover was cooperation between police forces, not an act by Myanmar against China.
2022-10-07: US announces export controls on advanced chips and chipmaking equipment

The US Bureau of Industry and Security announced controls covering specified advanced computing chips, supercomputer end uses and some chipmaking equipment. Equipment provisions took effect on 7 October, certain support by US persons on 12 October, and advanced computing and supercomputer controls on 21 October.
This was not a ban on every chip. On 12 December China requested WTO consultations with the US over the measures (DS615). A request for consultations is not a ruling that a measure is unlawful.
2019-05-16: US adds Huawei and 68 affiliates to the Entity List
The Commerce Department rule took effect on 16 May and appeared in the Federal Register on 21 May. It listed Huawei and 68 non-US affiliates in 26 destinations.

The rule imposed licensing requirements on exports, reexports and in-country transfers of items subject to US export regulations to the listed entities. It was separate from the extradition proceedings concerning Meng Wanzhou.
2018-12-01: Meng Wanzhou arrested in Vancouver: how the proceedings ended

Canadian authorities arrested Huawei’s chief financial officer at the request of the US. US prosecutors alleged fraud over representations to a bank concerning business in Iran. China’s foreign ministry described the case as political persecution.

On 24 September 2021, local time in Canada, Meng entered a deferred prosecution agreement with US prosecutors. The US withdrew its extradition request; Canada ended its proceedings and lifted her bail conditions. A US judge dismissed the indictment against Meng personally on 2 December 2022. The order did not dismiss the case against Huawei.
2016-07-12: South China Sea tribunal issues its award; China rejects it

The tribunal constituted at the Philippines’ request issued an award on maritime entitlements, the status of certain maritime features and conduct at sea. The Permanent Court of Arbitration served as registry.

The tribunal said it did not decide territorial sovereignty or delimit a maritime boundary. China’s foreign ministry called the award null and void and said China did not accept or recognise it. Read that position alongside the tribunal’s own account.
2012-09-11: Japan records the purchase of three islands; China objects

Japan announced its decision on 10 September. Its Diplomatic Bluebook dates the government’s purchase of three islands from a private owner to 11 September. China calls the islands Diaoyu Dao, Beixiao Dao and Nanxiao Dao.

China maintains the islands are Chinese territory and rejects the purchase. The date refers to a property transaction recorded by Japan, not a transfer of sovereignty agreed between the two countries.
2009-09-11: US announces three-year additional duties on certain Chinese tyres

The US president imposed additional duties for three years on certain passenger-vehicle and light-truck tyres from China. The White House cited market disruption and a safeguard in China’s WTO accession terms.
China requested WTO consultations on 14 September (DS399). The measure covered specified tyres, not all Chinese vehicles or all Chinese imports.
2001-04-01: US and Chinese military aircraft collide near Hainan

A Chinese naval J-8II fighter and a US Navy EP-3 surveillance aircraft collided near Hainan. Chinese pilot Wang Wei was killed; the damaged EP-3 landed on the island. The two governments gave different accounts of responsibility and the landing.
The 24 US crew members left China on 12 April. Their departure and the return of the aircraft were separate events: the EP-3 was later dismantled and taken home by cargo aircraft.
1999-05-07: NATO bombing hits the Chinese embassy in Belgrade; three journalists killed

The Chinese embassy in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was hit during NATO air strikes late on 7 May in Belgrade, already 8 May in Beijing. Chinese journalists Shao Yunhuan, Xu Xinghu and Zhu Ying were killed.

On 8 May the North Atlantic Council described the bombing as a mistake and expressed regret. China condemned the bombing and called for an investigation. The timeline uses the local date of the strike; the two dates refer to the same event.
1990-02-16: US statute continues suspension of munitions export licences for China

President George H. W. Bush signed the Foreign Relations Authorization Act for fiscal years 1990 and 1991 (Public Law 101-246). After the military crackdown on protests in Beijing in June 1989, the US had taken several measures against China. Section 902 codified some of them, including continued suspension of licences for exports to China of defence articles on the US Munitions List.

The word “continued” matters: this is the date of the statute, not the start of every restriction. The section provides exceptions and reporting conditions; it did not stop all trade between the two countries.
